summary:
Ameya Bhatawdekar, Field CTO at Braintrust, frames AI engineering as replatforming rather than iteration because model capability arrives in step functions, not increments. Dropping a new model into an architecture built around the previous model's limits forfeits the unlock, so architecture must follow model updates and evals must follow architecture. He grounds the talk in a notional site reliability agent with both read and write tools and traces five generations: (1) a single prompt whose evals measured final-answer quality, factuality, and hallucination against a golden dataset; (2) a RAG chain that added parser and retriever failure modes plus context-stuffing problems; (3) a 2023-era ReAct loop that fell short because models failed at tool-call arguments, orchestration, and long-context reasoning; (4) a workflow graph with classifier nodes and inter-node contracts that traded flexibility for control but expanded the eval surface; and (5) a modern looping agent enabled by mid-to-late 2025 model improvements in tool calling, planning, and long-horizon task handling.

This second section extends that story in three ways. First, because looping agents produce visibly different trajectories for the same input, the unit of eval shifts from a single run to a distribution, introducing pass-at-k (capability: did at least one of k attempts succeed?) and pass^(wedge)k (reliability: how many of k attempts succeeded?). Second, the system is no longer just a model in a loop but a product system augmented by memory (within and across sessions), robust code-execution sandboxes, MCP, and skill directories/symbolic-instruction repositories — each a new surface that old evals do not cover. Third, while the production-to-eval flywheel is universally accepted, in practice many teams run static evals and miss novel failure modes. Braintrust's Topics feature clusters production data to surface unanticipated failure categories so teams can extend eval coverage alongside architectural shifts. The closing takeaway is that durable evals, fed by production, are what keep working capabilities from breaking as new unlocks are integrated.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Replatforming, not iterating
sections.summary: Ameya introduces the idea that teams must replatform, not iterate, because model progress comes in step functions (tool use, long context, sandboxed code, memory) and dropping a new model into an architecture built around the old model's limitations forfeits the new capability unlock.

sections.title: Why you cannot just drop in a new model
sections.summary: Previous systems compensated for weak tool calling and other limitations; replacing the model without restructuring the system means you cannot tap into the new state of the art, so rearchitecting is required and evals must adapt accordingly.

sections.title: Grounding it in a site reliability agent
sections.summary: The five-generation walkthrough is grounded in a notional SR agent with both read and write tools (rollback, escalate, page) so the eval examples stay concrete.

sections.title: One prompt, one call, one answer to grade
sections.summary: The earliest apps were a single prompt with one model call; evals focused on final-answer accuracy, factuality, and hallucination using a golden dataset and scored definitions of good.

sections.title: The chain, and where retrieval goes wrong
sections.summary: RAG chains added pre-model steps and new failure points: the parser can extract the wrong field, the retriever can return the wrong context, and the model can be overwhelmed by stuffed context even when window sizes grew.

sections.title: The first ReAct loop, and why it fell short
sections.summary: Mid-2023 to early-2024 ReAct loops let the model reason and act step-wise, but models of that era failed at tool-call arguments, orchestration, and long-context reasoning, producing context collapse and falling short of the promise.

sections.title: Taking control back with workflow graphs
sections.summary: Faced with uncontrollable models, teams pulled orchestration into workflow graphs or state machines, letting models operate only at the node level for more reliability and predictability across known intents.

sections.title: The eval surface a graph creates
sections.summary: Graphs handle known intents well but break at the seams when users go off-script, so teams add complex special branches; this introduces branch-logic failures, broken inter-node contracts, and misfiring classifier nodes, demanding node-level evals and retry-loop checks in addition to overall orchestration scoring.

sections.title: Models get good enough to loop again
sections.summary: Mid-to-late 2025 model launches made tool calling extremely reliable and improved planning, long-horizon task handling, and course correction; the ReAct loop works again, but the same input now produces visibly different trajectories on every run.

sections.title: Pass at k for capability, the stricter one for reliability
sections.summary: Because looping agents show high trajectory variance, the unit of eval shifts from a single run to a distribution across k attempts. Pass-at-k asks whether at least one of k runs succeeds, measuring capability; pass^(wedge)k asks how many of k runs succeed, measuring reliability. A system can look strong on one and weak on the other, so teams must run the distribution rather than a single sample to understand capability vs. reliability.

sections.title: Memory, sandboxes, and skills around the loop
sections.summary: The agent is no longer just a model in a loop but a product system augmented by peripheral components: robust memory for within- and cross-session retrieval, code-execution sandboxes for running model-generated code, MCP for extensibility, and skill directories / symbolic instructions that continually augment model capabilities. Each is a new surface that the previous generation's evals do not cover, so partial coverage is the default if evals are not evolved with architecture.

sections.title: The flywheel most teams accept but never run
sections.summary: Everyone conceptually accepts the production-to-eval flywheel, but in practice most teams run static evals, miss novel failure modes, and get stagnant coverage — especially across generational shifts. Braintrust's Topics feature clusters production data to surface unanticipated failure categories so teams can expand eval coverage alongside architectural change. Ameya closes by urging durable, production-fed eval discipline: incremental improvements during incremental change and step-function improvements during replatforming are both supported only if the eval flywheel is actually running.
